Large Class & Extract Class

Learn to spot God Objects and apply Extract Class to regain Single Responsibility and testability.

Large classes increase risk, slow onboarding, and make tests fragile. Extraction restores clarity.

Identifying cohesive responsibilities, extracting classes, delegating, and keeping behavior intact.

Smaller classes, clearer tests, and components that change for one reason only.

Better reuse and safer refactors because functionality is no longer trapped in a single monolith.

screens.title: What is a Large Class (God Object)?
screens.narratorSegment: A Large Class, sometimes called a God Object, is a class that accumulates too many responsibilities, fields, and methods so that its purpose becomes vague. Concretely, you often see dozens of methods, many unrelated fields, or one class that seems to touch many parts of the system. An analogy is a Swiss Army knife that becomes so crowded it no longer fits in a pocket — useful in many ways but hard to use well in any single task. Symptoms include a long constructor with many parameters, methods that clearly belong to different domains, and repeated changes to the same file for unrelated features. The key definitional claim is that a Large Class violates the Single Responsibility Principle because it has multiple reasons to change. A common misconception is to confuse size with poor naming; a large class can be well-named yet still do too much. Use concrete checks: count related methods, trace change history to see multiple change reasons, and look for groups of methods that always change together. When you can name a cohesive responsibility and extract it, the large class has a candidate for refactoring. The takeaway is that size alone is a heuristic — the real issue is multiple responsibilities sharing one implementation.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A Large Class bundles multiple responsibilities, creating multiple reasons to change and reducing clarity.

content.html:
Core Concept › What is a Large Class?

Definition & Symptoms

A Large Class accumulates unrelated fields and behaviors and often violates SRP.

  • • Long constructors with many parameters and state.
  • • Dozens of methods that span different domains.
  • • Frequent unrelated changes in one file across features.
  • • Hard to unit test because of tangled dependencies.
Analogy

Like a Swiss Army knife stuffed with tools: flexible but difficult to use for focused work.

Key Takeaway

Look for multiple reasons to change — that is the true smell, not just physical size.

Quick Checklist

Change history
Do commits touch this class for unrelated features?
Cohesive groups
Are there groups of methods that always change together?
Test complexity
Do tests require heavy mocks and long setups?
Key Takeaway

A Large Class signals multiple responsibilities. Name the responsibilities before refactoring.

screens.title: How to detect a Large Class in practice
screens.narratorSegment: Detecting a Large Class is about evidence, not guesswork. Start with heuristic checks: many fields in the constructor, 20-plus methods or hundreds of lines, and multiple groups of methods that seem unrelated are red flags. Use version history: if the file appears in commits across unrelated features, that shows multiple reasons to change. Instrument a quick mental taxonomy: group methods by domain — profile, persistence, notifications, calculation — and see whether those groups form coherent units. If a group has its own state and several methods, it is a candidate for extraction. Also watch test complexity: when unit tests require heavy mocking or long setups just to exercise one behavior, that often means responsibilities are tangled. A common misconception is to equate class size with poor naming. In reality, a well-named class can still be handling too many changes. The practical approach is to gather a list of candidate responsibilities, estimate coupling between them, and select the smallest cohesive group for the first extraction. This conservative strategy reduces risk and lets you validate the design incrementally. How to detect a Large Class in practice means use constructor size, method grouping, commit history, and test complexity to find extraction candidates.. In practical terms, checklist, change-history signals, and quick heuristics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Symptoms › Detecting Large Class

Practical Checklist

  • • Long constructor or many fields suggesting mixed state.
  • • Multiple unrelated method groups present together.
  • • File appears across unrelated commits in version history.
  • • Unit tests are long, requiring many mocks or fixtures.
Heuristic

If you can name a new class around a set of methods and state, it's a valid extraction candidate.

Diagnosis Flow

Group methods

Cluster by domain and shared state to reveal cohesion pockets.

Inspect history

Check commits: does this file change for unrelated features?

Test shape

Long setup and many mocks indicate tangled responsibilities.

Key Takeaway

Combine structural checks with history and tests to confidently identify extraction targets.

screens.title: Why Large Classes hurt design
screens.narratorSegment: Large classes create practical problems that go beyond an aesthetic preference. First, maintainability suffers because a single change may require touching unrelated logic in the same class. This increases the chance of regression. For example, changing order processing in a class that also sends notifications could unintentionally alter notification state. Second, testability declines: unit tests must set up more state and mock more dependencies, making tests larger and more brittle. Teams often respond by skipping fine-grained tests, which reduces coverage and increases risk. Third, reuse is blocked because useful behavior is buried inside the monolith; extracting a notification manager makes it reusable in other places without dragging unrelated user logic along. Finally, Large Classes often violate SRP, which is foundational: a class with multiple reasons to change will inevitably entangle concerns. A common misconception is that extraction always increases coupling; when done with clear interfaces and minimal required data, extraction reduces coupling and improves cohesion. The practical effect is faster onboarding, smaller tests, and safer changes once extraction is applied appropriately. content.html:
Impact › Why Large Classes hurt

Three practical damages

Maintainability

Multiple reasons to change make safe edits hard; unrelated features get tangled into single commits.

Testability

Heavy setup and mocks make tests slow and brittle, reducing coverage and confidence.

Reusability

Useful behavior trapped inside a monolith cannot be reused without pulling unrelated code.

Key Takeaway

Extracting cohesive responsibilities reduces risk, shrinks tests, and frees logic for reuse.

Misconception Check

People often fear that extracting classes increases coupling. Done with clear interfaces and minimal required state, extraction reduces coupling and improves cohesion.

Practical rule

Extract when a group of methods shares state and represents a coherent responsibility.

screens.title: Extract Class: step-by-step
screens.narratorSegment: Extract Class is a straightforward refactoring when taken one small step at a time. Start by identifying a cohesive responsibility: find methods that operate on a shared subset of fields. Copy the relevant fields and methods into a new class and give it a clear name that reflects the role. Update the original class to hold an instance of the new class and delegate calls. Run tests after each small change. If tests fail, revert and narrow the extraction. Common refinements include moving only behavior that truly requires state into the new class, and updating access so the new class accepts necessary data via its constructor or methods rather than reaching into the original's internals. Keep the original class usable during the transition by adding thin delegation methods. A misconception to avoid is moving methods without their required state; always move state and behavior together. The safety rule is to perform small extractions, verify tests, and commit frequently. This keeps the refactor reversible and limits risk to a single responsibility at a time. Extract Class: step-by-step means identify a cohesive bundle, create a new class, move state and methods together, delegate, and test after each step.. In practical terms, a safe incremental workflow for extraction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Extraction workflow
keyIdea.text: Identify a cohesive bundle, create a new class, move state and methods together, delegate, and test after each step.

content.html:
Process › Extract Class Steps

Step-by-step

  1. Identify a cohesive responsibility by grouping methods and state.
  2. Create a new class named for that responsibility.
  3. Move the related fields and methods into the new class together.
  4. Replace original logic with delegation methods that forward calls.
  5. Run and update tests; commit each small successful change.
Safety tip

If a method needs state you didn't move, move the state too or refactor the method into a pure function.

Example heuristic

Pick the responsibility that appears the most cohesive and smallest first. That yields quick wins and reduces risk.

Key Takeaway

Small, test-backed extractions are the fastest path to safer design improvement.

screens.title: Criteria for extracting responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: Not every method or field should become its own class. Good extraction candidates share several practical traits. First, they operate on a set of fields that are not used elsewhere — that state should be moved with the methods. Second, the methods form a cohesive unit: they are conceptually part of the same role, such as order management or notification handling. Third, the extracted unit should have multiple methods or some state; single-method classes with no state are often better as functions or extracted methods. Fourth, extracting should reduce the number of reasons to change the original class. If extraction introduces a new reason to change across classes, reconsider the boundary or combine related pieces. Also prefer extraction that improves testability: if moving code allows you to write focused unit tests that were previously expensive, that’s a strong sign it’s the right extraction. A common mistake is over-extracting everything; aim for meaningful cohesion rather than mechanical splitting. Ultimately, testability, state locality, and real conceptual cohesion are the best guides. Criteria for extracting responsibilities means prefer cohesive groups that own state, improve testability, and reduce reasons to change the original class.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Decision › What to Extract

Good extraction signals

  • • Methods that operate on the same set of fields.
  • • A cohesive role name suggests a concept (e.g., OrderManager).
  • • Multiple methods or state — not a single stateless method.
  • • Extraction allows focused unit tests that were previously impractical.
Avoid

Don't extract tiny single-method classes without state. Prefer functions or method extraction in those cases.

Practical test

Ask: if I move these methods and their state into a class with a clear name, does the original class become simpler and easier to test?

Key Takeaway

Choose extraction that groups stateful behavior into a clearly named role and yields smaller tests.

content.html:
Code › User — original

Original User class (Python)

This class manages profile, orders and notifications together; note the mixed responsibilities.

class User:
  def __init__(self, user_id, username, email, address, phone):
    self.user_id = user_id
    self.username = username
    self.email = email
    self.address = address
    self.phone = phone
    self.orders = []  # List of order objects
    self.notification_settings = {'email': True, 'sms': False}

  # User Profile Methods
  def update_profile(self, new_email=None, new_address=None, new_phone=None):
    if new_email: self.email = new_email
    if new_address: self.address = new_address
    if new_phone: self.phone = new_phone
    print(f"User {self.username} profile updated.")

  def get_full_address(self):
    return f"{self.address}, {self.phone}"

  # Order Management Methods
  def add_order(self, order_details):
    self.orders.append(order_details)
    print(f"Order {order_details.order_id} added for {self.username}.")

  def get_order_history(self):
    return self.orders

  def calculate_total_spent(self):
    return sum(order.total_amount for order in self.orders)

  # Notification Methods
  def enable_email_notifications(self):
    self.notification_settings['email'] = True

Don't move methods without their associated state, or tests will break unexpectedly.

Which group appears smallest and most cohesive to extract first — orders or notifications?

Refactor › Extract Class — Refactored

Refactored Python classes

OrderManager and NotificationManager encapsulate their own state and behavior; User composes them.

class Order:
  def __init__(self, order_id, total_amount):
    self.order_id = order_id
    self.total_amount = total_amount

class OrderManager:
  def __init__(self, user_id):
    self.user_id = user_id
    self.orders = []

  def add_order(self, order_details):
    self.orders.append(order_details)
    print(f"Order {order_details.order_id} added for user {self.user_id}.")

  def get_order_history(self):
    return self.orders

  def calculate_total_spent(self):
    return sum(order.total_amount for order in self.orders)

class NotificationManager:
  def __init__(self, user_email, user_id):
    self.user_email = user_email
    self.user_id = user_id
    self.notification_settings = {'email': True, 'sms': False}

  def enable_email_notifications(self):
    self.notification_settings['email'] = True

  def send_welcome_email(self):
    print(f"Sending welcome email to {self.user_email} for user {self.user_id}.")

class User:
  def __init__(self, user_id, username, email, address, phone):
    self.user_id = user_id
    self.username = username
    self.email = email
    self.address = address
    self.phone = phone
    self.order_manager = OrderManager(user_id)
    self.notification_manager = NotificationManager(email, user_id)

  def update_profile(self, new_email=None, new_address=None, new_phone=None):
    if new_email: self.email = new_email; self.notification_manager.user_email = new_email
    if new_address: self.address = new_address
    if new_phone: self.phone = new_phone
Test advantage
You can now test order totals without creating notification state and vice versa.
API compatibility
Thin delegation methods keep external behavior stable during migration.

Migration note

Update dependent code gradually and add delegation methods to keep callers unchanged.

Key Takeaway

Composition keeps responsibilities separate while preserving observable behavior.

screens.title: Composition and Delegation
screens.narratorSegment: Composition is the act of a class holding instances of other classes to provide functionality rather than implementing every behavior itself. After Extract Class, the original class often becomes a thin coordinator that delegates responsibilities to composed objects. This pattern improves cohesion because each class has a single role and improves coupling because interactions are through small, defined interfaces. For example, User now has an order_manager instance responsible for orders. Delegation methods on User forward calls to order_manager so external code does not need to change immediately. A common misconception is that composition always makes the public A P I larger; in practice, you can selectively expose only the convenience methods and encourage callers to use the new manager classes when appropriate. Another practical point is data synchronization: when User updates an email, it should also update the notification manager's user_email field. This keeps state consistent and demonstrates that extraction often requires small coordination logic in the original class. screens.narratorSegment: A disciplined testing strategy is the backbone of safe Extract Class refactors. Begin by running the existing test suite to ensure a known-good baseline. Process › Testing Strategy

Safe testing steps

  • • Run full test suite to establish a baseline.
  • • Extract a single cohesive responsibility and add focused unit tests for the new class.
  • • Keep integration or end-to-end tests to confirm system behavior.
  • • Use delegation on the original class to preserve API compatibility.
  • • Commit frequently and revert if failures appear.
Common failure mode

Missing state or incorrect constructor arguments after moving methods causes test regressions. Move state and behavior together.

Testing tips

Prefer small fixtures, test the new class in isolation, and keep integration tests as a safety net.
Key Takeaway

Tests are your safety harness. Use them to guide and validate small, reversible extractions.

screens.title: Pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: When applying Extract Class, several traps commonly occur. First, don't create anemic domain models: avoid extracting every field into a class that becomes mere data with no behavior. Extract behavior with its state so the new class represents a meaningful role. Second, avoid over-extracting: creating tiny single-method classes increases complexity rather than reducing it. Use cohesion as your guide. Third, be careful not to break encapsulation by exposing too much of the original class internals; pass only the data required. Fourth, watch for increased coupling: if the new class depends heavily on the original internals, reconsider the boundary. Best practices include extracting small cohesive chunks, writing tests for the new class first if possible, and keeping delegation thin while migrating callers incrementally. Finally, remember context: if many classes are large across a codebase, extraction may not be enough — you might need an architectural change. These rules keep the refactor pragmatic and aligned with SRP and maintainability goals. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to recognize classes that have grown too large and how to use the Extract Class refactoring to restore clean design. Large classes, sometimes called God Objects, collect unrelated fields and methods until one class handles profiles, orders, notifications and more. That multiplies reasons to change and makes the code brittle. We will study symptoms — such as an explosion of fields, dozens of methods, and tangled responsibilities — and walk through a practical Python example where a User class is split into OrderManager and NotificationManager. Along the way you'll learn criteria for choosing which responsibilities to extract, how to preserve external behavior with delegation, and how to keep tests green during the change. This matters because smaller classes improve comprehension, enable focused unit tests, and help teams evolve features safely. By the end you will be able to spot the smell, design a safe extraction plan, and apply Extract Class in small increments. Consider the User example as a running case: it shows the concrete costs of a God Object and how composition returns clarity. Which responsibility would you extract first when reading a real large class?

These four objectives define what success looks like for this chapter. First, you will learn to identify the characteristics and symptoms of a Large Class, so you can quickly flag classes that carry multiple unrelated responsibilities. A concrete example is a user model that manages profile fields, order lists, and notification logic all at once. Second, you will understand the negative impacts of large classes on maintainability, testability and the Single Responsibility Principle. This helps you prioritize refactors and communicate technical debt. Third, you will apply the Extract Class refactoring to break a monolith into focused units. You will practice selecting cohesive methods and fields, performing the extraction, and using delegation to preserve behavior. Finally, you will determine practical criteria for new classes and recognize common challenges when breaking down code. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you recall the skill during code reviews and a verified competency milestone so you can measure your progress.

This companion objectives slide reframes the same four goals into practical checkpoints you can apply during refactors. First, when you see a class with a long list of unrelated fields or a dozen-plus methods, mark it for deeper review and note candidate responsibility clusters. Second, articulate the maintenance costs: explain how multiple reasons to change increase test complexity and coupling so stakeholders appreciate the risk. Third, practice the Extract Class technique in tiny steps: pick one cohesive responsibility, move data and behavior into a new class, adjust the original to delegate, run tests, and commit. Fourth, make pragmatic choices about what becomes a class: prefer new classes that hold state and multiple related methods; prefer functions for one-off behavior. Use small tests after each extraction to validate behavior. These checkpoints make extraction predictable and safe in real codebases.

A Large Class, sometimes called a God Object, is a class that accumulates too many responsibilities, fields, and methods so that its purpose becomes vague. Concretely, you often see dozens of methods, many unrelated fields, or one class that seems to touch many parts of the system. An analogy is a Swiss Army knife that becomes so crowded it no longer fits in a pocket — useful in many ways but hard to use well in any single task. Symptoms include a long constructor with many parameters, methods that clearly belong to different domains, and repeated changes to the same file for unrelated features. The key definitional claim is that a Large Class violates the Single Responsibility Principle because it has multiple reasons to change. A common misconception is to confuse size with poor naming; a large class can be well-named yet still do too much. Use concrete checks: count related methods, trace change history to see multiple change reasons, and look for groups of methods that always change together. When you can name a cohesive responsibility and extract it, the large class has a candidate for refactoring. The takeaway is that size alone is a heuristic — the real issue is multiple responsibilities sharing one implementation.

Detecting a Large Class is about evidence, not guesswork. Start with heuristic checks: many fields in the constructor, 20-plus methods or hundreds of lines, and multiple groups of methods that seem unrelated are red flags. Use version history: if the file appears in commits across unrelated features, that shows multiple reasons to change. Instrument a quick mental taxonomy: group methods by domain — profile, persistence, notifications, calculation — and see whether those groups form coherent units. If a group has its own state and several methods, it is a candidate for extraction. Also watch test complexity: when unit tests require heavy mocking or long setups just to exercise one behavior, that often means responsibilities are tangled. A common misconception is to equate class size with poor naming. In reality, a well-named class can still be handling too many changes. The practical approach is to gather a list of candidate responsibilities, estimate coupling between them, and select the smallest cohesive group for the first extraction. This conservative strategy reduces risk and lets you validate the design incrementally. How to detect a Large Class in practice means use constructor size, method grouping, commit history, and test complexity to find extraction candidates.. In practical terms, checklist, change-history signals, and quick heuristics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Large classes create practical problems that go beyond an aesthetic preference. First, maintainability suffers because a single change may require touching unrelated logic in the same class. This increases the chance of regression. For example, changing order processing in a class that also sends notifications could unintentionally alter notification state. Second, testability declines: unit tests must set up more state and mock more dependencies, making tests larger and more brittle. Teams often respond by skipping fine-grained tests, which reduces coverage and increases risk. Third, reuse is blocked because useful behavior is buried inside the monolith; extracting a notification manager makes it reusable in other places without dragging unrelated user logic along. Finally, Large Classes often violate SRP, which is foundational: a class with multiple reasons to change will inevitably entangle concerns. A common misconception is that extraction always increases coupling; when done with clear interfaces and minimal required data, extraction reduces coupling and improves cohesion. The practical effect is faster onboarding, smaller tests, and safer changes once extraction is applied appropriately. Why Large Classes hurt design means large classes increase regression risk, make tests brittle, and hide reusable functionality.. In practical terms, maintainability, testability, and reuse problems explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Extract Class is a straightforward refactoring when taken one small step at a time. Start by identifying a cohesive responsibility: find methods that operate on a shared subset of fields. Not every method or field should become its own class. Good extraction candidates share several practical traits. First, they operate on a set of fields that are not used elsewhere — that state should be moved with the methods. Second, the methods form a cohesive unit: they are conceptually part of the same role, such as order management or notification handling. Third, the extracted unit should have multiple methods or some state; single-method classes with no state are often better as functions or extracted methods. Fourth, extracting should reduce the number of reasons to change the original class. If extraction introduces a new reason to change across classes, reconsider the boundary or combine related pieces. Also prefer extraction that improves testability: if moving code allows you to write focused unit tests that were previously expensive, that’s a strong sign it’s the right extraction. A common mistake is over-extracting everything; aim for meaningful cohesion rather than mechanical splitting. When applying Extract Class, several traps commonly occur. First, don't create anemic domain models: avoid extracting every field into a class that becomes mere data with no behavior. Extract behavior with its state so the new class represents a meaningful role. Second, avoid over-extracting: creating tiny single-method classes increases complexity rather than reducing it. Use cohesion as your guide. Third, be careful not to break encapsulation by exposing too much of the original class internals; pass only the data required. Fourth, watch for increased coupling: if the new class depends heavily on the original internals, reconsider the boundary. Best practices include extracting small cohesive chunks, writing tests for the new class first if possible, and keeping delegation thin while migrating callers incrementally. Finally, remember context: if many classes are large across a codebase, extraction may not be enough — you might need an architectural change. These are the essential concepts to remember as you work through Large Class refactors. Large Class, or God Object, describes a class with many responsibilities and multiple reasons to change. The Single Responsibility Principle says each class should have only one reason to change; use it as a guiding constraint. Cohesion measures how well the elements inside a module belong together — high cohesion is the goal.
